title: Rigidity of the computably enumerable degrees
formal: Is every order automorphism of R, the c.e. Turing degrees, the identity?
definitions: A set A of natural numbers is computably enumerable (c.e.) if a finite ordinary Turing program enumerates exactly A. Write A≤_T B when an oracle Turing machine with membership access to B decides membership in A on every input. Equivalence under mutual reducibility defines a Turing degree. R is the set of degrees containing a c.e. set, ordered by ≤_T; it is not the set of all degrees below the halting problem. All quantification over degrees below is over R. The language has only ≤ and logical equality, with no named degrees or parameters unless explicitly stated. An order automorphism is an arbitrary bijection f:R→R such that a≤b iff f(a)≤f(b) for all a,b. No computability, definability, or continuity restriction is imposed on f. The assertion is ∀f∈Aut(R) ∀a∈R f(a)=a.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation, with exactly the structures and quantifiers specified here.
context: Parameter-free recovery of each degree by an arithmetic index would imply rigidity. Recovery only up to the double jump does not have that consequence.
why: Rigidity would say that the reducibility position of a computably enumerable degree determines the degree itself.

import_provenance.original_title: Rigidity of the computably enumerable degrees
import_provenance.original_statement: Is every order automorphism of the partially ordered set of computably enumerable Turing degrees the identity? This asks whether a computably enumerable degree is determined by its position in the reducibility ordering.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: Editorial continuation of Harrington–Shelah’s structural analysis, not a claim that Shelah personally posed this rigidity conjecture. The structure here is the c.e. degrees, not the full Turing degrees.

sentences: The objects are degrees of computably enumerable sets under Turing reducibility.
An automorphism preserves exactly the reducibility order.
The question forbids every nonidentity automorphism, including noncomputable ones.
Arithmetic coding of individual degrees would suffice, but is a stronger target.
The cited double-jump result does not distinguish every degree.
